standard.title: Usefulness and Reliability of Sources
standard.description: explain the usefulness of primary and secondary sources, and the reliability of the information as evidence
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain the usefulness and reliability of primary and secondary sources as evidence in a Year 9 historical inquiry, identifying bias and perspective.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the usefulness and reliability of primary and secondary sources as evidence, identifying absent perspectives, explaining bias and intent, corroborating across sources, and comparing sources for inconsistencies.

nodes.label: Bias, intent, and absent perspectives
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify perspectives absent from sources, explain the bias of an author and the intent of a source, and evaluate how each affects usefulness and reliability.
nodes.minimum_width: For at least one source, identify an absent perspective and explain how its absence affects the source's usefulness; explain the bias of the author and evaluate its effect on reliability.
nodes.typical_width: Identify perspectives absent from sources and evaluate the extent to which this affects usefulness; explain the bias of the author and the intent of a source and evaluate the extent to which this affects reliability; understand that bias does not disqualify a source — a biased source can be useful for revealing the attitudes of its author or period.
wider: Apply absent-perspective analysis to a topic where the historical record systematically excludes certain voices — such as First Nations experiences of frontier conflict, or women's perspectives on political events — examining what the pattern of absence reveals about how the historical record was constructed

Examine a source whose bias has been contested by historians — such as a government report or official history — analysing the debate about its reliability and what the debate reveals about how historical sources are evaluated
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who equate bias with uselessness cannot do the sophisticated source work required in Node 2 (corroboration) or in S06 and S07 (perspectives, contested interpretations). The insight that biased sources are useful for revealing the attitudes of their author or period is foundational to professional historical source analysis.

response_modes.reason: Explicitly teach the distinction between 'this source is biased' and 'this source is not useful'. Model how a biased source can be highly useful for revealing the perspectives, attitudes or intentions of the author — reframing bias from a disqualifier to an analytical opportunity.

success_criteria: Identify at least one perspective absent from a source and explain how its absence affects the source's usefulness
Explain the bias of the author of a source and evaluate its effect on reliability
Explain why a biased source is not necessarily a useless source, using a specific example

nodes.label: Corroboration and question-dependent usefulness
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can determine the usefulness of sources by corroborating with other sources and explain how the usefulness and reliability of a source depends on the questions asked of it.
nodes.minimum_width: Corroborate information from at least two sources and explain how the usefulness of each changes depending on the question asked.
nodes.typical_width: Determine usefulness by corroborating with other sources of information — verifying or questioning claims by triangulating across multiple sources; examine that the reliability and usefulness of a source depends on the questions asked of it — for example, an account with a particular historical perspective can be useful for revealing past prevailing attitudes even if unreliable as a factual record; determine whether information in one source can be verified by information in another; compare a range of sources and identify similarities, differences and inconsistencies in interpretations.
wider: Apply corroboration across sources that present contradictory accounts of the same event — examining how historians navigate evidentiary conflict and what it means when sources cannot be reconciled

Apply question-dependent usefulness analysis to a propaganda source — examining how its reliability as a factual record is low but its usefulness as evidence of the attitudes of its producers or audience is high

response_modes.reason: Corroboration and question-dependent usefulness bring together origin/context analysis (S03) and bias/perspective analysis (Node 1) into a fully integrated source evaluation framework. This is where the individual analytical skills combine into professional-level historical source work.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Question-dependent usefulness is a powerful analytical concept that transforms how students engage with all sources throughout the course — enabling them to make productive use of sources they might otherwise dismiss. It directly develops the S07 skill of analysing contested interpretations.
success_criteria: Corroborate information from at least two sources and explain what the comparison reveals
Explain how the usefulness of a specific source changes depending on which question it is asked to answer
Identify at least one inconsistency between sources and explain what it suggests about the reliability of one or both
